VERDICT: EXTEND C0001 | `scan_health()` currently sets `tools_available[tool_name] = True` whenever the runner returns without raising. This is not just a missing-binary problem. `_run_tool()` also returns sentinel `CompletedProcess(..., returncode=-1, stderr="TIMEOUT")` on timeout, and each runner currently converts that into `[]`, so timed-out tools are also reported as available and healthy. This contaminates the same availability signal consumed by `HealthScan.tools_available` and can mislead round control into believing the health scan completed normally when a tool never produced output.

VERDICT: MERGE C0004 <- F001 | Root cause matches C0001/C0004 exactly: tool availability is inferred from “runner did not raise” instead of actual execution status, which mislabels both NOT_FOUND and TIMEOUT as available.

FINDING_ID: F002
SEVERITY: 0.91
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.62
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()` does not actually sandbox test execution against the patched code. It writes only the patched target file into a temp directory under its basename (`patched_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, os.path.basename(target_path))`) and then runs `test_cmd` with `cwd=tmpdir`, but it never rewrites the command to point at that patched file/tree and never copies the rest of the project into the sandbox. In the integration path shown in `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()`, the command is `["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...]`. From the temp dir, that path usually does not exist, so tests either fail spuriously or run against the original repository via external paths/import resolution rather than the patched file. Evidence in endocrine.py: only one file is written into tmpdir; no package tree mirroring, no path remap, no env isolation, no source-root copy.
FOLLOW: This breaks the module’s key promised capability: “sandbox-test proposed fixes (SAFE/HARMFUL/NEUTRAL)” and “no source modification.” Downstream, `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()` marks findings `verified=True` when endocrine returns SAFE or NEUTRAL. If tests are executed against the wrong codebase, a harmful fix can be marked verified, which then crosses interfaces into NK bug-closed logic and causes future duplicate findings about the still-unfixed bug to be auto-closed. That is a silently wrong result, not just weak test coverage.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — sandbox the project root, not just the single file: create a temp copy of the relevant source tree (at minimum the directory containing `target_path`, preserving relative path), write the patched file back into the mirrored location, and run `test_cmd` against that mirrored tree so imports and pytest paths resolve to sandboxed code only.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F003
SEVERITY: 0.86
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58
DESCRIPTION: FIND — fix verdict computation can classify a fix as SAFE even when it introduces new issues in one tool, as long as it removes more issues in another. `_compute_fix_verdict()` sums signed deltas into `total_net = net_type_errors + net_ruff_errors + net_bandit_issues` and returns HARMFUL only if `total_net > 0`. Example from current logic: `+3` new bandit issues, `-5` ruff issues, `0` type errors gives `total_net = -2`, so verdict becomes SAFE even though security regressions were introduced. This violates the docstring claim “HARMFUL: new issues introduced.”
FOLLOW: Downstream, `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()` treats SAFE/NEUTRAL as programmatic verification and marks the finding `verified=True`. Because the verdict collapses heterogeneous regressions into one scalar, a fix that worsens security or type safety can be accepted and then propagated into the bug-closed path for later rounds. That produces a silent false closure and can suppress legitimate rediscovery of the bug.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — treat any positive per-tool delta as HARMFUL before considering aggregate improvement: if `net_type_errors > 0 or net_ruff_errors > 0 or net_bandit_issues > 0`, return HARMFUL; only return SAFE when all per-tool deltas are `<= 0` and at least one is `< 0` or tests pass.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F004
SEVERITY: 0.81
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.47
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_find_target_file()` can patch the wrong file because it matches any extracted `*.py` token by substring containment: `if sp_path.endswith(match) or match in sp_path`. A mention like `brain.py` matches any source path containing that substring anywhere, and if multiple files share a basename/suffix the first incidental match wins. It also searches both description and proposed fix text, so a fix example mentioning another file can redirect patching away from the actual target. The function then falls back to `source_paths[0]`, which can silently select an unrelated file.
FOLLOW: `evaluate_fix()` uses this path to choose baselines, apply edits, and compute verdicts. If the wrong file is selected, the evaluator may fail to apply a valid fix, mark it UNEVALUABLE, or worse, apply a textual replacement to a different file and then report SAFE/HARMFUL on irrelevant diagnostics. Downstream, this corrupts immune-stage fix verification and can falsely verify or reject findings.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — resolve targets only by exact normalized basename or exact relative/absolute path match against `source_paths`; if the match is ambiguous or absent, return `None` and mark the fix UNEVALUABLE instead of falling back to the first source file.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F005
SEVERITY: 0.76
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.41
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()` baselines and post-fix counts are not comparable for tools whose diagnostics depend on project context. Pre-fix counts are gathered on the original file path in the real repository; post-fix counts are gathered on an isolated temp file with only the basename present. For pyright/mypy especially, imports, config discovery, and neighboring modules can change diagnostic counts depending on location. The code then subtracts these counts as if they are same-environment measurements.
FOLLOW: This can produce false deltas in either direction: the patched temp file may lose import context and appear to gain errors unrelated to the fix, or lose project-context checks and appear cleaner than the original. Since verdicts rely on these net deltas, endocrine can mark fixes HARMFUL or SAFE for environmental reasons instead of actual code change. That directly affects `verified=True` propagation in the immune pipeline.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — run both pre-fix and post-fix tool counts in the same sandboxed project layout. Copy the target context into tempdir first, run baseline tools there on the unmodified sandbox file, then overwrite with the patch and rerun tools in the same location.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F006
SEVERITY: 0.68
FLAW_CLASS: 4
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.33
DESCRIPTION: FIND — the advertised “Health scan — static analysis (pyright/ruff/bandit) between rounds” does not actually surface tool execution failure as a diagnostic or status field separate from availability. When a tool times out or emits unparsable output, runners return `[]` and `scan_health()` just aggregates an empty result set. Aside from the already-registered availability bug, there is no diagnostic record or failure counter telling the caller that the scan was incomplete. Evidence: parse failures only log warnings; `HealthScan` contains counts and `tools_available` but no per-tool run status / error reason.
FOLLOW: A zero-diagnostic health scan can mean “clean code” or “tool failed,” and the insect brain receives no machine-readable distinction. That can suppress pacing/escalation decisions tied to code health and makes the endocrine report misleading during infrastructure failures. In PoC terms this is a silent wrong result in the monitoring layer, because the feature appears to fire cleanly while having skipped analysis.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — add a minimal per-tool status field to `HealthScan` (e.g. `tool_status[tool] = "ok" | "not_found" | "timeout" | "parse_error" | "failed"`) and populate it from `_run_tool` / runner parse branches so incomplete scans are explicitly visible.
VERIFIED: TRUE
